---
title: "Coercion in Rust"
---


## 1. The big idea

A **coercion** is an implicit type conversion that the compiler inserts for you. Rust is deliberately stingy with these. Compared with C#, it has:

- no implicit numeric widening (`i32` won't become `i64` on its own),
- no user-defined `implicit operator`,
- only a short, fixed list of conversions, mostly about pointers and references.

```rust
let a: i32 = 5;
let b: i64 = a;          // ❌ mismatched types
let b: i64 = a as i64;   // ✅ explicit cast
let b: i64 = a.into();   // ✅ explicit conversion via From/Into
```

Coercions also only happen at specific **coercion sites**, where the compiler already knows the *expected* type:

```
 Coercion sites (expected type is known)
 ─────────────────────────────────────────────
 let x: Target = expr;          // annotated let
 f(expr)                        // function / method argument
 Struct { field: expr }         // struct field initializer
 return expr / tail expression  // function return
 static / const X: T = expr;
```

## 2. The coercion catalog

```
 ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
 │ 1. Mutability weakening   &mut T      →  &T                    │
 │ 2. Deref coercion         &U          →  &T   (U: Deref<T>)    │
 │ 3. Unsized coercion       &[T; N]     →  &[T]                  │
 │                           &Concrete   →  &dyn Trait            │
 │ 4. Fn item / closure      fn item     →  fn pointer            │
 │ 5. Never type             !           →  any T                 │
 │ (6. Raw pointer forms     &T → *const T,  &mut T → *mut T)     │
 └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

### 2.1 Mutability weakening: `&mut T → &T`

You can always give up write access, but you can never gain it.

```rust
fn read(x: &i32) { println!("{x}"); }

let mut n = 10;
let r: &mut i32 = &mut n;
read(r);          // ✅ &mut i32 → &i32

// The reverse (&T → &mut T) never happens. That would break the borrow rules.
```

### 2.2 Deref coercion: `&U → &T`

If `U` implements `Deref<Target = T>`, then `&U` coerces to `&T`. The compiler applies this **repeatedly** until the types match.

```rust
fn greet(name: &str) { println!("Hello, {name}"); }
fn total(xs: &[i32]) -> i32 { xs.iter().sum() }

let s = String::from("KS");
greet(&s);                     // &String → &str

let v = vec![1, 2, 3];
total(&v);                     // &Vec<i32> → &[i32]

let b: Box<String> = Box::new("LB".to_string());
greet(&b);                     // &Box<String> → &String → &str  (2 hops!)
```

```
   &Box<String> ──Deref──▶ &String ──Deref──▶ &str
        │                     │                  │
   Box::deref()        String::deref()       target ✓
```

Common `Deref` implementations in the standard library:

| Type `U` | `Deref::Target` | So `&U` coerces to |
|---|---|---|
| `String` | `str` | `&str` |
| `Vec<T>` | `[T]` | `&[T]` |
| `Box<T>` | `T` | `&T` |
| `Rc<T>` / `Arc<T>` | `T` | `&T` |
| `PathBuf` | `Path` | `&Path` |
| `OsString` | `OsStr` | `&OsStr` |

Deref coercion has three mutability variants:

```
 &U      → &T       requires  U: Deref<Target=T>
 &mut U  → &mut T   requires  U: DerefMut<Target=T>
 &mut U  → &T       requires  U: Deref<Target=T>   (also weakens mutability)
```

### 2.3 Unsized coercion: sized becomes dynamically sized

This turns a pointer to something with a compile-time-known size into a **fat pointer** to something whose size is only known at runtime.

**Array to slice:**

```rust
let arr: [i32; 3] = [10, 20, 30];
let s: &[i32] = &arr;             // &[i32; 3] → &[i32]
```

```
 &[i32; 3]  (thin pointer)          &[i32]  (fat pointer)
 ┌──────┐                          ┌──────┬───────┐
 │ ptr  │                          │ ptr  │ len=3 │   ← length moves
 └──────┘                          └──────┴───────┘     from type to runtime
  length "3" lives in the TYPE
```

**Concrete type to trait object:**

```rust
trait Shape { fn area(&self) -> f64; }
struct Circle { r: f64 }
impl Shape for Circle { fn area(&self) -> f64 { 3.14159 * self.r * self.r } }

let c = Circle { r: 2.0 };
let s: &dyn Shape = &c;                       // &Circle → &dyn Shape
let b: Box<dyn Shape> = Box::new(Circle { r: 1.0 }); // Box<Circle> → Box<dyn Shape>
```

```
 &dyn Shape (fat pointer)
 ┌──────┬────────┐
 │ data │ vtable │──▶ ┌──────────────┐
 └──┬───┴────────┘    │ size, align  │
    ▼                 │ drop_in_place│
  Circle{r:2.0}       │ area() ──────┼──▶ Circle::area
                      └──────────────┘
```

This works through `&`, `&mut`, `Box`, `Rc`, `Arc`, raw pointers, and `Pin` (they implement the `CoerceUnsized` trait). So `Box<[i32; 3]>` also coerces to `Box<[i32]>`.

### 2.4 Function items and closures to `fn` pointers

Every named function has its own unique, zero-sized type. It coerces to a plain function pointer when needed. A closure that **captures nothing** does too.

```rust
fn add_one(x: i32) -> i32 { x + 1 }
fn times_two(x: i32) -> i32 { x * 2 }

let ops: [fn(i32) -> i32; 3] = [add_one, times_two, |x| x - 3];
//                               ^fn item  ^fn item   ^non-capturing closure
```

A closure that captures variables cannot become an `fn` pointer. For those, you use `impl Fn` or `Box<dyn Fn>`.

### 2.5 The never type `!` coerces to anything

Expressions that never produce a value (`panic!`, `return`, `continue`, `loop {}` with no break) have type `!`, which fits wherever a type is expected:

```rust
let n: i32 = match input.parse() {
    Ok(v)  => v,                 // i32
    Err(_) => panic!("bad"),     // ! → i32
};
```

## 3. Don't confuse coercion with method-call auto-deref

The dot operator has its **own** mechanism. It auto-references and auto-dereferences the receiver until it finds a matching method:

```rust
let v = vec![1, 2, 3];
let r = &&&v;
r.len();        // compiler tries &&&Vec, &&Vec, &Vec, Vec, [i32]... finds [T]::len
```

```
 Coercion           → happens at a coercion site, needs an expected type
 Auto-deref (dot)   → happens on method receivers, searches for the method
```

They feel similar, but auto-deref works even in places where coercion wouldn't.

## 4. Where coercion does NOT happen (common gotchas)

**Gotcha 1: generic trait bounds.** Coercion needs a known target type, and a generic `T` is inferred from the argument rather than fixed in advance:

```rust
trait Shout { fn shout(&self); }
impl Shout for &str { fn shout(&self) { println!("{}!", self.to_uppercase()); } }

fn call<T: Shout>(x: T) { x.shout(); }

let s = String::from("hi");
call(&s);          // ❌ T = &String, and &String doesn't impl Shout
call(s.as_str());  // ✅ be explicit
call(&*s);         // ✅ also explicit: deref String → str, then borrow
```

**Gotcha 2: no coercion inside containers.** Coercion applies to the outer pointer, not to the elements:

```rust
let names: Vec<String> = vec!["a".into(), "b".into()];
let v: &[String] = &names;          // ✅ &Vec<String> → &[String]
let w: &[&str]  = &names;           // ❌ String elements won't become &str
let w: Vec<&str> = names.iter().map(|s| s.as_str()).collect(); // ✅ explicit
```

**Gotcha 3: branches need a common type.** For `if`/`match` arms, the compiler tries to find a common type, but it often needs your annotation to know you want `dyn`:

```rust
struct Square { a: f64 }
impl Shape for Square { fn area(&self) -> f64 { self.a * self.a } }

let shape = if big { Box::new(Circle { r: 5.0 }) } else { Box::new(Square { a: 1.0 }) };
// ❌ Box<Circle> vs Box<Square>

let shape: Box<dyn Shape> = if big { Box::new(Circle { r: 5.0 }) }
                            else   { Box::new(Square { a: 1.0 }) };
// ✅ the expected type drives both arms to coerce
```

## 5. Design takeaways

Since you value clean API design, here are the practical lessons.

**Accept the "borrowed, unsized" form in parameters.** Because of coercion, the most general parameter type is the most convenient for callers:

| Instead of | Prefer | Callers can pass |
|---|---|---|
| `&String` | `&str` | `&String`, `&str`, `&Box<str>`, string literals |
| `&Vec<T>` | `&[T]` | `&Vec<T>`, `&[T; N]`, `&Box<[T]>` |
| `&PathBuf` | `&Path` | `&PathBuf`, `&Path` |
| `&Box<T>` | `&T` | almost anything holding a `T` |

Clippy will flag the left-column versions with the `ptr_arg` lint. This is the Rust flavor of "depend on the narrowest abstraction you need."

**Implement `Deref` only for smart-pointer-like types.** Since `Deref` is the *only* user-extensible implicit conversion, it's tempting to abuse it to fake inheritance (for example, `impl Deref for Employee { type Target = Person; }`). This is a known anti-pattern ("Deref polymorphism"). It makes method resolution surprising and hides the relationship. For "is-a" style reuse, prefer traits; for "has-a," prefer composition with explicit delegation.

**Prefer explicit conversions for value changes.** Use `From`/`Into`, `TryFrom`, or `as`. Coercion in Rust is about *viewing* data differently (through a different kind of pointer), never about silently changing the data itself.
